name: Amoxicillin
adultDose: 1 g once daily (severe diarrhoea, severe upper UTI); 2 g once daily (severe CAP, sepsis, bone and joint infections, intra-abdominal infections, hospital-acquired pneumonia, severe enteric fever); meningitis 2 g every 12h (WHO AWaRe 2022, Table 49.1, p.633). Gonorrhea: 1 g IM single dose (WHO 2024)
pediatricNote: WHO weight bands (oral, per dose, every 12h): 3 to <6 kg 250 mg; 6 to <10 kg 375 mg; 10 to <15 kg 500 mg; 15 to <20 kg 750 mg; >=20 kg 500 mg every 8h or 1 g every 12h. WHO states a maximum daily dose of 1.5 g, which can be higher for serious bacterial infections. Source: WHO AWaRe antibiotic book 2022, pp.152 and 640.
duration: Pneumonia, children: 3 days if low HIV prevalence and no chest indrawing; 5 days if high HIV prevalence and chest indrawing (AWaRe 2022, p.152). Mild CAP, adults: 5 days (AWaRe 2022, p.150). Other indications: see the AWaRe book.
notes: Pediatric dose follows the WHO AWaRe Antibiotic Book (2022) oral weight-band table for mild to moderate pneumonia (80-90 mg/kg/day). Not a first-choice antibiotic for UTI or skin infections under AWaRe. Can take with or without food.

rules.message: Weight is below 3 kg. The WHO amoxicillin weight-band table (AWaRe 2022, p.152) starts at 3 kg. Do not use this calculator; follow neonatal or specialist guidance.

name: Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX)
pediatricNote: Treatment (UTI, infectious diarrhoea), WHO weight bands, every 12h: 3 to <6 kg 120 mg; 6 to <10 kg 240 mg; 10 to <30 kg 480 mg; >=30 kg adult dose 960 mg (total co-trimoxazole per dose; AWaRe 2022, p.651). AWaRe also states a maximum daily dose of 1200 mg of the sulfamethoxazole component. HIV prophylaxis (once daily): <6mo or <5kg 120mg; 6mo–5y or 5–15kg 240mg; 6–14y or 15–30kg 480mg; >14y or >30kg 960mg
duration: Lower UTI, adults: 3 days (usually 5 days in pregnancy and 7 days in men); children: 3 days (AWaRe 2022, chapter 23, p.283 for children). HIV prophylaxis: long-term. Other indications: see the AWaRe book.
notes: Pediatric treatment dose is total co-trimoxazole (4mg TMP/kg = 24mg co-trimoxazole/kg). HIV prophylaxis (WHO 2014): adults 960mg once daily, continued regardless of pregnancy stage; also reduces malaria in people with HIV. Not recommended by WHO for shigellosis (resistance). Caution in G6PD deficiency.

rules.message: Weight is below 3 kg. The WHO co-trimoxazole weight-band table (AWaRe 2022, p.651) starts at 3 kg. Do not use this calculator; follow neonatal or specialist guidance.
Not for neonates under 4 weeks (kernicterus risk). HIV-exposed infants start co-trimoxazole prophylaxis at 4–6 weeks.

name: Metronidazole
adultDose: 500 mg every 8h (C. difficile, intra-abdominal infections, necrotizing fasciitis); 750 mg every 8h for amoebic abscess; 500 mg every 12h for trichomoniasis; single dose 500 mg (surgical prophylaxis) or 2 g (trichomoniasis) (WHO AWaRe 2022, Table 49.1, p.636)
pediatricNote: WHO weight bands (oral/IV, every 8h): 3 to <6 kg 30 mg; 6 to <10 kg 50 mg; 10 to <15 kg 100 mg; 15 to <20 kg 150 mg; 20 to <30 kg 200 mg; >=30 kg adult dose 500 mg (AWaRe 2022, p.649). Children: 7.5 mg/kg every 8h, maximum daily dose 1 g. Amoebic abscess: 10-15 mg/kg every 8h.
notes: Use with caution in the 1st trimester of pregnancy (follow national formulary). C. difficile: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are preferred where available; metronidazole 500mg every 8h for 10 days is an alternative for non-severe disease only. Avoid alcohol during treatment and 48h after. Metallic taste is common.

rules.message: Weight is below 3 kg. The WHO metronidazole weight-band table (AWaRe 2022, p.649) starts at 3 kg. Do not use this calculator; follow neonatal or specialist guidance.
Pregnancy: use with caution in the 1st trimester (follow national formulary).

name: ORS (Oral Rehydration Salts)
adultDose: As much as wanted (about 200–400ml after each loose stool)
pediatricNote: Plan A (after each loose stool): < 2y 50–100ml; 2–10y 100–200ml; older: as much as wanted. Plan B: 75ml/kg over 4h, then reassess.
notes: WHO low-osmolarity ORS (245 mOsm/L). 1 sachet + 1L clean water. Severe dehydration (Plan C): give IV fluids first. If IV is not possible, children can be given ORS by nasogastric tube (or by mouth if able to drink): 20 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours (total 120 mL/kg), reassessing every 1-2 hours; give it more slowly if there is repeated vomiting or increasing abdominal distension. Refer urgently (WHO IMCI 2019). Do not apply this rate to adults. Give ORS by mouth as soon as the patient can drink. In severe acute malnutrition use ReSoMal instead (except suspected cholera).

name: Zinc sulfate
adultDose: Not recommended by WHO for adults
notes: Give alongside ORS for all children under 5 with diarrhea. Not needed for children receiving zinc-fortified therapeutic foods (F-75, F-100, RUTF).

name: Vitamin A
adultDose: No routine supplementation for adults. For xerophthalmia or measles in adults, follow national guidance.
pediatricFreq: single dose (measles: day 1 & 2; eye signs: day 1, 2 & 14)
duration: Single dose (measles: 2 doses; eye signs of deficiency: 3 doses)
indications: SAM (only if therapeutic foods are not fortified)
contraindications: Pregnancy or possible pregnancy: never give a single dose > 25,000 IU (teratogenic)
notes: SAM (WHO 2013): no high-dose vitamin A if the child receives WHO-standard F-75, F-100 or RUTF. Give one age-based dose on admission only if foods are not fortified; repeat on day 2 and 14 only with eye signs or recent measles. Postpartum supplementation is not recommended by WHO.

rules.message: Pregnant or possibly pregnant: never give a high-dose capsule (> 25,000 IU). Maximum 10,000 IU/day or 25,000 IU/week (WHO 2011).

name: Mebendazole
notes: WHO 2017 preventive chemotherapy: 500mg single dose once or twice yearly depending on prevalence; pregnant women may be treated after the 1st trimester. Pinworm is not covered by the dose calculated above (that is the STH dose). Pinworm: 100mg as a single dose, repeated after 2 weeks (CDC, manufacturer label); treat household contacts at the same time; limited data under 2 years. Can be crushed and mixed with food.

rules.message: Not for children under 1 year (WHO preventive chemotherapy starts at 12 months).

name: Artemether-lumefantrine (AL / Coartem)
pediatricNote: Tablets of 20/120mg: 5–<15kg: 1 tab; 15–<25kg: 2 tabs; 25–<35kg: 3 tabs; ≥35kg: 4 tabs — all × 6 doses at 0, 8, 24, 36, 48, 60h. With 40/240mg tablets, halve the tablet count.
notes: Preferred treatment in all trimesters of pregnancy, including the 1st trimester (WHO, Nov 2022). Infants < 5kg: use the dedicated infant formulation (Coartem Baby, dispersible tablets of 2.5mg/30mg, for 2–<5kg) — do not split older-child tablets. Dose studied in infants of 2 to <5kg (CALINA): 2 tablets (5mg/60mg) twice daily for 3 days; check the product label. Must be taken with food — fat increases absorption. Complete the full course.

rules.message: Under 5 kg: use the infant formulation (Coartem Baby, dispersible tablets of 2.5mg/30mg, for 2–<5 kg) — do not use standard tablets.

name: Ciprofloxacin
pediatricNote: WHO weight bands (oral, every 12h): 3 to <6 kg 50 mg; 6 to <10 kg 100 mg; 10 to <15 kg 150 mg; 15 to <20 kg 200 mg; 20 to <30 kg 300 mg; >=30 kg adult dose 500 mg (AWaRe 2022, p.646). WHO maximum daily dose 1.5 g oral. Shigellosis: 3 days (WHO 2005: 15mg/kg every 12h). Cholera: 20mg/kg single dose (max 1g).
duration: Typhoid (enteric fever), low fluoroquinolone resistance: 7 days mild, 10 days severe, if improved and afebrile for 48 h (AWaRe 2022, chapter 15; in high-resistance areas AWaRe uses azithromycin or ceftriaxone instead). Shigellosis: 3 days; cholera: single dose.
contraindications: Avoid in children unless benefit > risk
notes: Cholera (GTFCC 2022): doxycycline is first-line for all ages including pregnant women; ciprofloxacin or azithromycin are alternatives. Antibiotics only for eligible cholera patients (e.g. severe dehydration). Fluoroquinolone resistance in S. Typhi is widespread — check local data. Give 2h before or 4–6h after zinc, antacids or dairy.

rules.message: Weight is below 3 kg. The WHO ciprofloxacin weight-band table (AWaRe 2022, p.646) starts at 3 kg. Do not use this calculator; follow neonatal or specialist guidance.
Pregnancy: use only if no safer alternative. For cholera, doxycycline or azithromycin are preferred (GTFCC 2022).

name: Ceftriaxone
pediatricNote: Severe pneumonia, sepsis and other severe infections: 80 mg/kg once daily. Meningitis: 100 mg/kg once daily (WHO AWaRe 2022, Table 50.1, p.645). Maximum daily dose 3 g (AWaRe 2022). The WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children (2013) allows up to 4 g/day for meningitis (100 mg/kg once daily or 50 mg/kg every 12h).
contraindications: Premature neonates up to 41 weeks postmenstrual age
notes: Pediatric dosing per WHO AWaRe antibiotic book 2022 (Table 50.1, p.645); see also the WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children (2013). The calculated dose is the 80 mg/kg dose (maximum 3 g/day). Meningitis needs the higher dose of 100 mg/kg, so check the note above. Gonorrhea: WHO 2024 recommends 1g IM single dose. Reconstitute 1g in 3.5ml 1% lidocaine for IM (less pain; never IV). IV: dilute in 50-100ml NS over 30 min.

rules.message: Neonates need a different regimen: 50mg/kg every 12h if < 7 days old, 75mg/kg after 1 week (meningitis, with gentamicin). Contraindicated in premature neonates (up to 41 weeks postmenstrual age), neonatal jaundice, or with IV calcium-containing fluids — use cefotaxime instead.
